q: A 28-year-old man falls on his shoulder and sustains a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus. He cannot abduct the arm beyond the first few degrees, and sensation is lost over the lower half of the deltoid. Which nerve is injured?
e: The axillary nerve (C5, C6) winds round the surgical neck of the humerus. It supplies deltoid and teres minor, and through the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm it supplies the skin over the lower deltoid (the 'regimental badge' area). The first ~15 degrees of abduction come from supraspinatus (suprascapular nerve), so only that small arc survives.
p: Humerus fracture → nerve: surgical neck = axillary; spiral groove (midshaft) = radial; supracondylar = median (anterior interosseous branch); medial epicondyle = ulnar.

q: Clawing of the ring and little fingers is more marked when the ulnar nerve is cut at the wrist than when it is cut at the elbow. This is called:
e: A lesion at the elbow also paralyses the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus, so the distal interphalangeal joints flex less and the claw looks milder. A lesion at the wrist spares FDP, so the unopposed long flexors produce more obvious clawing.
p: Froment sign = adductor pollicis weakness (thumb IP flexion by FPL substitutes). Wartenberg sign = abducted little finger (palmar interossei weak).

q: In most individuals, the artery to the sinoatrial node arises from the:
e: The SA nodal artery arises from the right coronary artery in about 60% of people and from the circumflex branch of the left coronary artery in the rest.
p: The AV nodal artery comes from the artery that gives the posterior interventricular branch, which is the RCA in right-dominant hearts (most people). So inferior MI (RCA) often causes heart block.

q: A 30-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis cannot adduct her right eye on looking to the left, and her left eye shows nystagmus when abducting. Convergence is normal. The lesion lies in the:
e: This is internuclear ophthalmoplegia. The medial longitudinal fasciculus links the abducens nucleus of one side to the medial rectus subnucleus of the other side. A lesion of the right MLF stops the right eye adducting on left gaze. Convergence is intact because it uses a separate pathway to the oculomotor nucleus, which shows the oculomotor nerve itself is fine.
p: INO is named for the side that fails to adduct. Bilateral INO in a young adult suggests multiple sclerosis; in an older person, think brainstem stroke.

q: Which intrinsic muscle of the larynx is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve?
e: All intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve except cricothyroid, which is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. Cricothyroid tenses the vocal cords.
p: The external laryngeal nerve runs close to the superior thyroid artery, so it is at risk when that artery is ligated in thyroidectomy. Injury gives a weak, low-pitched voice. Posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor of the vocal cords.

q: The anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) is formed by the:
o: Free border of the lesser omentum
e: Anteriorly lies the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) containing the portal vein, hepatic artery proper and common bile duct. Posteriorly lies the IVC, superiorly the caudate process of the liver, and inferiorly the first part of the duodenum.
p: Pringle manoeuvre = compressing the hepatoduodenal ligament at the epiploic foramen to control bleeding from the liver.

q: The stapes is derived from which pharyngeal arch?
e: Reichert cartilage of the second arch forms the stapes, styloid process, stylohyoid ligament, and the lesser horn and upper body of the hyoid. Meckel cartilage of the first arch forms the malleus and incus.
p: Arch nerves: 1st = mandibular (V3), 2nd = facial (VII), 3rd = glossopharyngeal (IX), 4th and 6th = vagus (X). The 3rd arch forms the greater horn and lower body of the hyoid.

q: A patient stands on the right leg and the pelvis drops on the left side. The nerve most likely damaged is the:
e: This is a positive Trendelenburg sign. Gluteus medius and minimus of the stance (right) side normally hold the pelvis level, and both are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve. When they are weak, the unsupported opposite side drops.
p: The side that drops is the normal side; the lesion is on the stance side. Inferior gluteal nerve injury weakens gluteus maximus, so climbing stairs and rising from a chair are hard.

q: Cannon 'a' waves in the jugular venous pulse are characteristically seen in:
e: The 'a' wave is produced by atrial contraction. In complete heart block the atrium sometimes contracts against a closed tricuspid valve (AV dissociation), giving intermittent large cannon waves. In atrial fibrillation there is no 'a' wave at all.
p: Large 'v' wave = tricuspid regurgitation. Steep 'y' descent (Friedreich sign) = constrictive pericarditis. Absent 'a' wave = atrial fibrillation.

q: In an upright person, the ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) ratio is highest at the:
e: Both ventilation and perfusion increase from apex to base, but perfusion rises more steeply. So V/Q is highest at the apex (about 3) and lowest at the base (about 0.6).
p: High V/Q and high PO2 at the apex suit Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which is why reactivation TB favours the apices.

q: The substance considered the gold standard for measuring glomerular filtration rate is:
e: Inulin is freely filtered and is neither secreted nor reabsorbed, so its clearance equals GFR. Creatinine is slightly secreted and overestimates GFR. PAH is used to measure renal plasma flow.
p: Clearance = UV/P. Glucose clearance is normally zero; PAH clearance is roughly equal to effective renal plasma flow.

q: Which hormone acts through the JAK-STAT pathway?
e: Growth hormone, prolactin, erythropoietin and many cytokines bind receptors that activate JAK kinases. Insulin uses a receptor tyrosine kinase, glucagon uses Gs-cAMP, and aldosterone uses an intracellular nuclear receptor.
p: Receptors for prolactin, EPO, GH, thrombopoietin, G-CSF and the interleukins all signal through JAK-STAT.

q: The absolute refractory period of a nerve fibre is mainly due to:
e: After opening, voltage-gated Na+ channels enter an inactivated state (inactivation gate closed) and cannot reopen until the membrane repolarises. During this time no stimulus, however strong, can trigger a new action potential.
p: Relative refractory period = some Na+ channels have recovered, and K+ conductance is still high. A stronger-than-normal stimulus can fire the nerve.

q: Cholecystokinin is secreted by which cells?
o: I cells of the duodenum and jejunum
G cells of the gastric antrum
e: I cells release CCK in response to fatty acids and amino acids. CCK contracts the gallbladder, relaxes the sphincter of Oddi and stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion.
p: S cells = secretin (bicarbonate). G cells = gastrin. K cells = GIP. L cells = GLP-1. D cells = somatostatin.

q: Which of the following shifts the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve to the LEFT?
e: Carbon monoxide raises haemoglobin's affinity for the oxygen it still carries, shifting the curve left and impairing oxygen release to tissues. Raised CO2, H+, temperature and 2,3-BPG all shift the curve to the right (Bohr effect).
p: Right shift = 'CADET face Right': CO2, Acid, 2,3-DPG, Exercise, Temperature. Left shift: fetal Hb, CO, methaemoglobin, alkalosis, hypothermia.

q: Sleep spindles and K-complexes are characteristic of which sleep stage?
e: Stage N2 shows sleep spindles (12-14 Hz bursts) and K-complexes. N1 shows theta waves, N3 shows delta (slow-wave) activity, and REM shows a low-voltage mixed pattern with sawtooth waves.
p: Most of an adult's sleep is spent in N2. Night terrors and sleepwalking occur in N3; nightmares occur in REM.

q: An infant has hepatomegaly, severe fasting hypoglycaemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia and hyperlipidaemia. The deficient enzyme is most likely:
e: Von Gierke disease (GSD type I) blocks the final step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, so the liver cannot release free glucose. The accumulated glucose-6-phosphate is diverted to lactate, uric acid and triglycerides.
p: Pompe (II) = acid maltase, cardiomegaly. Cori (III) = debranching enzyme, milder with no lactic acidosis. McArdle (V) = muscle phosphorylase, exercise cramps and myoglobinuria.

q: The rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis is:
e: HMG-CoA reductase converts HMG-CoA to mevalonate. It is the committed, regulated step and the target of statins.
p: The same intermediate, HMG-CoA, is made by mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase for ketone body synthesis, while cytosolic HMG-CoA feeds cholesterol synthesis.

q: A 3-day-old boy becomes lethargic and is found to have hyperammonaemia, low plasma citrulline and increased urinary orotic acid. The most likely deficiency is:
e: In OTC deficiency, carbamoyl phosphate builds up and spills into the cytosol, where it enters pyrimidine synthesis and produces orotic acid. CPS-I deficiency has hyperammonaemia without orotic aciduria. OTC deficiency is X-linked and is the most common urea cycle disorder.
p: Orotic aciduria with hyperammonaemia = OTC deficiency. Orotic aciduria without hyperammonaemia but with megaloblastic anaemia = UMP synthase deficiency (hereditary orotic aciduria).

q: Thiamine status is best assessed by measuring the activity of which red cell enzyme?
e: Transketolase in the HMP shunt needs thiamine pyrophosphate. Low erythrocyte transketolase activity, rising with added TPP, indicates thiamine deficiency.
p: Erythrocyte glutathione reductase measures riboflavin (B2). Erythrocyte aminotransferase measures pyridoxine (B6). FIGLU excretion after a histidine load reflects folate status.

q: A boy with developmental delay, choreoathetosis, self-biting of lips and fingers, and gouty arthritis most likely has a deficiency of:
e: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked absence of HGPRT. The purine salvage pathway fails, de novo purine synthesis increases, and uric acid is overproduced. It presents with self-mutilation and neurological features.
p: ADA deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). Xanthine oxidase deficiency lowers uric acid and can cause xanthine stones.

q: Western blotting is used to detect:
e: Western blot separates proteins by gel electrophoresis and detects them with antibodies. Southern blot detects DNA and Northern blot detects RNA.
p: Mnemonic SNOW DROP: Southern = DNA, Northern = RNA, Western = Protein. South-Western = DNA-binding proteins.

q: Macrophages with 'crumpled tissue paper' cytoplasm in the bone marrow are seen in deficiency of:
e: Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disorder. Glucocerebroside accumulates in macrophages (Gaucher cells), causing hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain and pancytopenia.
p: Sphingomyelinase = Niemann-Pick (foamy cells, cherry-red spot). Hexosaminidase A = Tay-Sachs (cherry-red spot, no hepatosplenomegaly). Alpha-galactosidase A = Fabry (X-linked).

q: A competitive inhibitor alters enzyme kinetics by:
o: Increasing Km with no change in Vmax
Decreasing Vmax with no change in Km
Increasing Vmax with no change in Km
e: A competitive inhibitor competes for the active site. Enough substrate overcomes it, so Vmax is unchanged, but more substrate is needed to reach half-maximal velocity, so the apparent Km rises.
p: Non-competitive: Vmax falls, Km unchanged. Uncompetitive: both Km and Vmax fall. On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, competitive inhibitor lines meet on the y-axis.

q: Which mediator acts on the hypothalamus to raise the thermoregulatory set point in fever?
e: Pyrogens such as IL-1 and TNF induce cyclo-oxygenase in the hypothalamus. The resulting prostaglandin E2 raises the set point. NSAIDs reduce fever by blocking prostaglandin synthesis.
p: Pain = PGE2 + bradykinin. Leukotriene B4 = neutrophil chemotaxis. Histamine = the main mediator of the immediate increase in vascular permeability.

q: Psammoma bodies are characteristically seen in all of the following EXCEPT:
e: Psammoma bodies are concentric, laminated calcifications (dystrophic calcification) typical of papillary architecture. They are seen in papillary thyroid carcinoma, serous ovarian tumours, meningioma and mesothelioma, but not in follicular carcinoma.
p: Mnemonic PSaMMoma: Papillary thyroid, Serous ovarian, Meningioma, Mesothelioma.

q: The most common protein defect in hereditary spherocytosis involves:
e: Ankyrin mutations are the most frequent cause of hereditary spherocytosis, followed by band 3, spectrin and protein 4.2. Loss of vertical membrane linkages makes the cells spherical, and they are trapped in the spleen.
p: In HS, MCHC is raised and osmotic fragility is increased. The eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding test is highly sensitive. Splenectomy is curative for the anaemia.

q: The translocation t(15;17) is associated with:
e: t(15;17) produces the PML-RARA fusion protein, which blocks myeloid differentiation at the promyelocyte stage. Patients often present with DIC. All-trans retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide induce differentiation.
p: t(9;22) = CML (BCR-ABL). t(8;14) = Burkitt (MYC). t(14;18) = follicular lymphoma (BCL2). t(11;14) = mantle cell lymphoma (cyclin D1).

q: Apple-green birefringence under polarised light is seen with which stain in amyloidosis?
e: Amyloid takes up Congo red, appearing pink-red under ordinary light and apple-green under polarised light. This reflects its cross-beta-pleated sheet structure.
p: Abdominal fat pad aspiration is a simple first biopsy. AL amyloid = light chains (myeloma). AA amyloid = serum amyloid A (chronic inflammation).

q: Which ultrastructural change indicates IRREVERSIBLE cell injury?
o: Large flocculent amorphous densities in mitochondria
Detachment of ribosomes from the endoplasmic reticulum
e: Flocculent densities in mitochondria reflect severe mitochondrial damage and mark the point of no return, along with membrane rupture and nuclear changes (pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis). Swelling, blebbing and ribosome detachment are reversible.
p: The two hallmarks of irreversibility are inability to restore mitochondrial function and profound plasma membrane damage.

q: In minimal change disease, the characteristic finding on electron microscopy is:
o: Diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes
Splitting of the glomerular basement membrane
e: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. Light microscopy is normal, and EM shows diffuse effacement of foot processes. It responds well to steroids.
p: Spike and dome = membranous nephropathy. Wire loops = lupus nephritis (class IV). 'Basket-weave' GBM splitting = Alport syndrome.

q: Classic Reed-Sternberg cells of classical Hodgkin lymphoma typically express:
e: Classical RS cells are CD15+ and CD30+ and are usually negative for CD45 and CD20. In nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, the 'popcorn' (LP) cells are CD20+ and negative for CD15 and CD30.
p: Nodular sclerosis is the most common subtype of classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Mixed cellularity is associated with EBV. Lymphocyte-depleted has the worst prognosis.

q: A 7-year-old has typical absence seizures with 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges on EEG and no other seizure types. The preferred first-line drug is:
e: Ethosuximide blocks T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons, which drive absence seizures. Valproate is preferred if generalised tonic-clonic seizures also occur. Carbamazepine and phenytoin can worsen absence seizures.
p: Drugs that can aggravate absence or myoclonic seizures: carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin, vigabatrin.

q: The specific antidote for heparin overdose is:
e: Protamine is strongly basic and binds the acidic heparin to form an inactive complex. It fully reverses unfractionated heparin and only partly reverses LMWH.
p: Warfarin = vitamin K, plus prothrombin complex concentrate when urgent. Dabigatran = idarucizumab. Factor Xa inhibitors = andexanet alfa.

q: Which drug shows zero-order (saturation) kinetics within or near its therapeutic range?
e: Phenytoin's metabolising enzymes saturate near therapeutic concentrations. A small dose increase can then cause a disproportionate rise in plasma level and toxicity. Therapeutic drug monitoring is used.
p: Zero-order kinetics: phenytoin, ethanol, high-dose aspirin. A fixed AMOUNT of drug is eliminated per unit time, not a fixed fraction.

q: Flushing and an erythematous rash over the face, neck and upper trunk during a rapid intravenous infusion is characteristic of:
e: Vancomycin infusion reaction ('red man' or 'red neck' syndrome) is caused by direct, non-IgE histamine release from mast cells. It is prevented by infusing over at least 60 minutes and can be eased with antihistamines.
p: Other vancomycin adverse effects: nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Oral vancomycin is not absorbed and is used for C. difficile colitis.

q: Which first-line antitubercular drug causes optic neuritis with red-green colour blindness?
e: Ethambutol causes dose-related retrobulbar optic neuritis. Visual acuity and colour vision should be checked, and it is used with caution in young children who cannot report visual symptoms.
p: INH = peripheral neuropathy (give pyridoxine) and hepatitis. Rifampicin = orange urine and enzyme induction. Pyrazinamide = hyperuricaemia and hepatotoxicity.

q: An antiarrhythmic drug that causes pulmonary fibrosis, hypo- or hyperthyroidism, corneal microdeposits and blue-grey skin discoloration is:
e: Amiodarone is iodine-rich and lipophilic with a very long half-life. It affects thyroid, lung, liver, cornea and skin. Baseline and periodic thyroid, liver and lung assessment is advised.
p: Despite prolonging QT, amiodarone rarely causes torsades de pointes. It has class I, II, III and IV actions.

q: In organophosphate poisoning, the drug that regenerates acetylcholinesterase (if given before 'ageing' of the enzyme) is:
e: Oximes such as pralidoxime remove the phosphoryl group from the inhibited enzyme and reactivate it, mainly reversing nicotinic effects such as muscle weakness. Atropine blocks muscarinic effects but does not reactivate the enzyme.
p: Titrate atropine to drying of bronchial secretions, not to pupil size or heart rate. Oximes are ineffective in carbamate poisoning.

q: The principal mechanism by which metformin lowers blood glucose is:
e: Metformin activates AMP-activated protein kinase and mainly suppresses hepatic glucose output. It does not cause hypoglycaemia when used alone and is weight-neutral.
p: Metformin causes lactic acidosis rarely; it is avoided when eGFR is below 30. Long-term use can cause vitamin B12 deficiency.

q: On KOH mount of a sinus biopsy, thin septate hyphae with acute-angle (about 45 degrees) dichotomous branching are seen. The likely fungus is:
e: Aspergillus produces narrow, septate hyphae with regular acute-angle dichotomous branching. Mucorales produce broad, ribbon-like, pauci-septate hyphae branching at wide (often right) angles.
p: Mucormycosis: think diabetic ketoacidosis and rhino-orbito-cerebral disease with a black eschar; treat with amphotericin B plus surgical debridement. Voriconazole is first-line for invasive aspergillosis.

q: A capsulated yeast is seen with India ink staining of the CSF of an HIV-positive patient with meningitis. The organism is:
e: India ink (negative staining) shows the polysaccharide capsule of Cryptococcus as a clear halo around the yeast. Cryptococcal antigen testing of CSF or serum is more sensitive.
p: Cryptococcus: urease-positive, grows on bird-seed (niger seed) agar with brown colonies, and is the commonest cause of fungal meningitis in AIDS.

q: A positive CAMP test is characteristic of:
e: Group B Streptococcus produces CAMP factor, which enhances the beta-haemolysis of Staphylococcus aureus, producing an arrowhead-shaped zone of haemolysis.
p: GBS is a leading cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis. It is hippurate-hydrolysis positive and bacitracin-resistant. S. pyogenes is bacitracin-sensitive and PYR-positive.

q: During the 'window period' of acute hepatitis B infection, the only detectable serological marker is:
e: In the window period HBsAg has disappeared but anti-HBs is not yet detectable. IgM antibody to the core antigen is present throughout this phase.
p: Anti-HBs alone = vaccinated. Anti-HBs plus IgG anti-HBc = recovered from past infection. HBsAg for more than 6 months = chronic infection.

q: The biological indicator used to check the efficiency of an autoclave is spores of:
e: Spores of Geobacillus (formerly Bacillus) stearothermophilus are highly resistant to moist heat, so their destruction confirms autoclave efficacy.
p: Hot air oven = Bacillus atrophaeus (formerly B. subtilis var niger). Ionising radiation = Bacillus pumilus. Standard autoclave cycle = 121 degrees C at 15 psi for 15 minutes.

q: Crescent (banana-shaped) gametocytes on a peripheral smear are characteristic of:
e: P. falciparum gametocytes are crescent-shaped. Other features include multiple ring forms per RBC, appliqué forms and Maurer's dots, with usually only rings and gametocytes seen in peripheral blood.
p: P. vivax: enlarged RBCs with Schüffner's dots. P. malariae: band forms and quartan fever. P. vivax and ovale form hypnozoites, so primaquine or tafenoquine is needed for radical cure.

q: The tuberculin (Mantoux) test is an example of which type of hypersensitivity?
e: The Mantoux reaction is a delayed-type (cell-mediated) hypersensitivity mediated by sensitised T cells and macrophages. It is read at 48-72 hours as induration.
p: Type I = IgE (anaphylaxis). Type II = antibody against cell-surface antigen (transfusion reaction). Type III = immune complex (serum sickness, Arthus reaction). Type IV = T cell (contact dermatitis, Mantoux).

q: 'Medusa head' colonies on nutrient agar are characteristic of:
e: B. anthracis forms rough colonies with curled outgrowths at the edge, described as Medusa-head colonies. Gelatin stab culture shows an 'inverted fir tree' pattern. It is non-motile, capsulated and spore-forming.
p: McFadyean reaction (polychrome methylene blue) shows the capsule of B. anthracis. Cutaneous anthrax produces a painless black eschar ('malignant pustule').

q: Among the voluntary muscles, rigor mortis first appears in the:
e: Rigor mortis follows a proximal-to-distal sequence (Nysten's rule) in voluntary muscles: eyelids first, then face, jaw, neck, trunk and upper limbs, then lower limbs, with fingers and toes last. Involuntary muscle (myocardium) stiffens even earlier.
p: Rigor typically starts 1-2 hours after death in temperate climates, is fully developed by about 12 hours and passes off in roughly the same order. Cadaveric spasm is instant stiffening without primary relaxation.

q: Which feature of a ligature mark favours hanging over ligature strangulation?
o: Oblique, non-continuous mark above the thyroid cartilage
Mark at or below the thyroid cartilage
e: In hanging the ligature mark runs obliquely upward towards the knot and is usually incomplete at the knot. A strangulation mark is horizontal, encircles the neck completely and usually lies at or below the thyroid cartilage.
p: Fracture of the hyoid and thyroid cartilage, along with neck bruising, is more typical of throttling (manual strangulation). Dribbling of saliva from the angle of the mouth suggests antemortem hanging.

q: Postmortem caloricity (a rise in body temperature after death) is classically seen in deaths from:
e: Postmortem caloricity occurs where heat production was raised before death or bacterial activity continues: cholera, septicaemia, tetanus, strychnine poisoning and heat stroke.
p: Algor mortis = postmortem cooling. Livor mortis (hypostasis) begins at about 1-2 hours and becomes fixed at about 6-8 hours.

q: Tattooing around a firearm entry wound is caused by:
o: Unburnt and partly burnt powder particles
e: Powder grains embedded in the skin cause tattooing (stippling), which cannot be wiped off and indicates a close-range shot. Smoke blackening can be wiped off and indicates an even closer range. Burning and singeing come from the flame.
p: Contact wounds show a muzzle imprint, and on bone may show a cherry-red track from carboxyhaemoglobin. Exit wounds are usually larger and everted, without soot or tattooing.

q: The preferred antidote in methanol poisoning is:
e: Fomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing conversion of methanol to formaldehyde and formic acid, which cause metabolic acidosis and optic nerve damage. Ethanol is an alternative competitive substrate. Haemodialysis removes methanol and formate.
p: Methanol attacks the optic nerve and retina (blindness, 'snowfield' vision). Folinic acid speeds formate clearance.

q: Transverse white lines across the nails (Aldrich-Mees lines) in chronic poisoning are classically associated with:
e: Chronic arsenic poisoning causes Mees lines, raindrop pigmentation, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis and peripheral neuropathy. Arsenic deposits in hair and nails, which can be analysed long after exposure.
p: Lead = Burton's (blue) gum line, basophilic stippling, wrist and foot drop. Mercury = erethism, acrodynia, and 'mad hatter' tremor.

q: Gustafson's method of age estimation is based on:
e: Gustafson described six regressive changes in teeth for estimating age in adults: attrition, periodontosis, secondary dentine, cementum apposition, root resorption and root transparency.
p: Root transparency is considered the most reliable of Gustafson's criteria. Pubic symphysis changes (Todd's method) also estimate adult age.

q: 'Every contact leaves a trace' is the basis of:
e: Locard's principle holds that the perpetrator and the scene or victim exchange material such as fibres, hair, soil or blood. This underpins the collection of trace evidence.
p: The McNaughten rule concerns the legal test of insanity. Chain of custody must be documented for every item of trace evidence.

q: Sensitivity of a screening test is calculated as:
e: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive, i.e. true positives out of all who truly have the disease.
p: Specificity = TN/(TN+FP). PPV = TP/(TP+FP). NPV = TN/(TN+FN). SnNout: a highly Sensitive test that is Negative rules disease out.

q: A study starts with people who have a disease and people who do not, then looks back at their past exposure. The measure of association used is:
e: This is a case-control study. Because incidence cannot be calculated, the odds ratio is used to estimate relative risk, a good approximation when the disease is rare.
p: Cohort study: starts with exposure, measures incidence, gives relative and attributable risk. Case-control studies are good for rare diseases; cohort studies are good for rare exposures.

q: If disease prevalence in the screened population increases while the test itself stays the same, which value rises?
e: Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test and do not change with prevalence. A higher prevalence raises the positive predictive value and lowers the negative predictive value.
p: This is why screening targeted at high-risk groups yields fewer false positives per true case.

q: Herd immunity does NOT protect unvaccinated people against:
e: Tetanus is not transmitted from person to person; infection comes from spores in the environment. Immunising others therefore gives no indirect protection.
p: Each person must be protected individually against tetanus. Elimination of maternal and neonatal tetanus depends on immunising pregnant women and on clean delivery practices.

q: Under India's vitamin A prophylaxis programme, a child aged 9-12 months receives:
e: The first dose of 1,00,000 IU is given at 9 months with measles-rubella vaccination. Doses of 2,00,000 IU follow every 6 months up to 5 years of age, making 9 doses in total.
p: Vitamin A deficiency eye signs: night blindness is the earliest symptom, Bitot spots are seen on the conjunctiva, and keratomalacia is a medical emergency.

q: The Horrocks apparatus is used to estimate:
e: The Horrocks apparatus uses bleaching powder solution and starch-iodide indicator to estimate the amount of bleaching powder needed to disinfect a given volume of water, such as a well.
p: Residual chlorine is tested with the orthotolidine (OT) test. The recommended free residual chlorine is 0.5 mg/L after a contact time of 1 hour.

q: In the 'iceberg phenomenon' of disease, the submerged part of the iceberg represents:
o: Undiagnosed and subclinical cases in the community
e: The visible tip is the clinical cases a doctor sees. The submerged portion is the hidden mass of undiagnosed, subclinical and carrier states, which is what screening tries to detect.
p: Diseases with a large hidden portion (e.g. hypertension, diabetes, anaemia) are good candidates for screening programmes.

q: Which vaccine is most sensitive to heat?
e: OPV is the most heat-sensitive vaccine in routine use. It is stored frozen at district level and above and kept at +2 to +8 degrees C at the point of use. The vaccine vial monitor shows heat exposure.
p: Freeze-sensitive vaccines that must never be frozen include hepatitis B, pentavalent, DPT, TT/Td and PCV. The shake test detects freeze damage in adsorbed vaccines.

q: In the left ear, Rinne test is negative and the Weber test lateralises to the left. The most likely diagnosis is:
e: Negative Rinne means bone conduction is better than air conduction, which indicates conductive loss. In conductive loss, Weber lateralises to the affected ear.
p: Weber goes to the worse ear in conductive loss and to the better ear in sensorineural loss. A false-negative Rinne occurs with severe unilateral SNHL due to transcranial transfer of sound to the other ear.

q: The most common site of epistaxis is:
o: Little's area on the anteroinferior nasal septum
e: Little's area contains Kiesselbach's plexus, an anastomosis of the anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine and superior labial (septal branch) arteries. It is exposed to drying and trauma.
p: Woodruff's plexus (posterior, beneath the inferior turbinate) is a source of posterior epistaxis in older, hypertensive adults.

q: In otosclerosis, the Carhart notch on bone-conduction audiometry is seen at:
e: Stapes fixation produces an artefactual dip in bone conduction, maximal at 2000 Hz. It disappears after successful stapes surgery.
p: Noise-induced hearing loss shows a notch at 4000 Hz. Otosclerosis typically shows paracusis Willisii (hearing better in noise) and a Schwartze sign (flamingo-pink flush on the promontory).

q: Gradenigo syndrome consists of ear discharge, deep retro-orbital pain and:
e: Gradenigo syndrome results from petrous apicitis. The inflammation involves the abducens nerve in Dorello's canal (lateral rectus palsy and diplopia) and the trigeminal ganglion (retro-orbital pain).
p: Petrous apicitis is a complication of otitis media; CT or MRI confirms it.

q: Quinsy is a collection of pus in the:
e: Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) lies between the tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor muscle. It causes trismus, a 'hot potato' voice, and displacement of the uvula to the opposite side.
p: Incise at the most bulging point or where a line along the base of the uvula meets a line along the anterior pillar. Interval tonsillectomy is usually done about 6 weeks later.

q: An abscess deep to the sternocleidomastoid following mastoiditis is called:
e: Pus breaks through the medial surface of the mastoid tip and tracks deep to the sternocleidomastoid, producing a Bezold abscess.
p: Citelli = along the posterior belly of digastric. Luc = deep to temporalis via the external auditory canal. Postauricular abscess is the most common mastoid abscess.

q: Anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary antrum on imaging (Holman-Miller sign) is characteristic of:
e: JNA arises near the sphenopalatine foramen and expands into the pterygopalatine fossa, pushing the posterior antral wall forward. It occurs in adolescent boys with recurrent profuse epistaxis and nasal obstruction.
p: Biopsy is avoided in suspected JNA because of the risk of torrential bleeding. Diagnosis is by contrast CT or MRI. Treatment is surgical excision after preoperative embolisation.

q: A 35-year-old develops sudden onset unilateral lower motor neuron facial weakness with no other findings. The most appropriate initial management within 72 hours is:
e: For Bell's palsy, oral prednisolone started within 72 hours improves recovery. Eye care (lubricants, taping at night) prevents exposure keratitis. Antivirals alone are not recommended.
p: About 70-85% of patients recover fully. Forehead sparing suggests an upper motor neuron (central) lesion, not Bell's palsy.

q: The definitive treatment for acute primary angle-closure glaucoma, once the pressure has been controlled, is:
e: After medical lowering of IOP (IV acetazolamide, topical beta-blocker, pilocarpine, hyperosmotic agents), laser peripheral iridotomy relieves pupillary block. A prophylactic iridotomy is also done in the fellow eye.
p: Mydriatics such as atropine can precipitate angle closure in an eye with a narrow angle.

q: Sudden painless loss of vision with a pale, oedematous retina and a cherry-red spot at the macula suggests:
e: In CRAO the ischaemic inner retina becomes opaque and white, while the fovea, which is thin and supplied by the choroid, keeps its red colour.
p: Central retinal vein occlusion has a 'blood and thunder' fundus. A cherry-red spot also occurs in Tay-Sachs and Niemann-Pick disease.

q: Koeppe nodules at the pupillary margin are a sign of:
e: Granulomatous uveitis shows mutton-fat keratic precipitates and iris nodules: Koeppe nodules at the pupillary margin and Busacca nodules on the iris surface.
p: Causes of granulomatous uveitis include sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, syphilis and Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease.

q: The most common cause of blindness in India is:
e: National blindness surveys in India have consistently found cataract to be the leading cause of blindness. Uncorrected refractive error is the leading cause of visual impairment.
p: India's blindness programme (NPCBVI) prioritises cataract surgery with intraocular lens implantation.

q: A relative afferent pupillary defect is best detected by:
e: When the light swings from the normal eye to the affected eye, both pupils dilate (Marcus Gunn pupil), because less light signal reaches the midbrain from the damaged optic nerve or retina.
p: RAPD indicates an optic nerve lesion (e.g. optic neuritis) or extensive retinal disease. It does not occur with cataract or refractive error.

q: Herbert's pits are a feature of:
e: Herbert's pits are depressions at the limbus left by healed limbal follicles, and are pathognomonic of trachoma (Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes A-C).
p: WHO SAFE strategy: Surgery for trichiasis, Antibiotics (azithromycin), Facial cleanliness, Environmental improvement. Arlt's line is scarring of the upper tarsal conjunctiva.

q: A young man has a painful red eye with photophobia, circumcorneal (ciliary) congestion, a small sluggish pupil and normal intraocular pressure. The most likely diagnosis is:
e: Anterior uveitis produces ciliary flush, photophobia and a miosed pupil from iris sphincter spasm. Angle closure gives a mid-dilated fixed pupil with high IOP. Conjunctivitis gives superficial congestion with a normal pupil.
p: Treat with topical steroids and cycloplegics (which relieve pain and prevent posterior synechiae). Recurrent acute anterior uveitis in a young man suggests HLA-B27 disease, e.g. ankylosing spondylitis.

q: The standard testing distance for a Snellen chart is:
e: At 6 metres the light rays from the chart are practically parallel, so accommodation is not needed.
p: Each Snellen letter subtends 5 minutes of arc at its specified distance, and each limb of the letter subtends 1 minute.

q: A haemodynamically stable patient has a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 180/min that persists after vagal manoeuvres. The drug of choice is:
e: Adenosine briefly blocks AV nodal conduction, terminating re-entrant supraventricular tachycardias that involve the AV node. It is given as a rapid IV bolus with a saline flush.
p: Adenosine causes transient chest discomfort and flushing. Its effect is reduced by theophylline and increased by dipyridamole. Use with caution in severe asthma.

q: The most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia in adults is:
e: Pneumococcus remains the most frequently identified bacterial cause of CAP. It typically causes lobar consolidation with rusty sputum.
p: Klebsiella: alcoholics, 'red currant jelly' sputum, bulging fissure. Staph aureus: post-influenza, cavities and pneumatoceles. CURB-65 grades CAP severity.

q: Which set of findings fits SIADH?
o: Hyponatraemia, euvolaemia, inappropriately concentrated urine with urine sodium >30 mmol/L
Hyponatraemia with oedema and low urine sodium
e: In SIADH excess ADH retains water, causing dilutional hypotonic hyponatraemia in a clinically euvolaemic patient. Urine is inappropriately concentrated and urinary sodium remains high.
p: Treat with fluid restriction first. Correct chronic hyponatraemia slowly (generally ≤10 mmol/L in 24 hours) to avoid osmotic demyelination. Small cell lung cancer is a classic cause.

q: In adult diabetic ketoacidosis, the first step in management is usually:
o: IV insulin bolus before any fluids
e: Patients with DKA are markedly fluid-depleted. Initial resuscitation with isotonic saline restores volume and lowers glucose. Fixed-rate IV insulin follows. Check potassium before insulin, because insulin drives K+ into cells.
p: If serum potassium is below 3.3 mmol/L, replace it before starting insulin. Add dextrose when glucose falls to about 250 mg/dL. Bicarbonate is reserved for severe acidosis (pH below about 6.9).

q: Hemisection of the spinal cord (Brown-Séquard syndrome) produces below the lesion:
o: Ipsilateral weakness and loss of proprioception, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature
Contralateral weakness with ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature
Bilateral loss of pain and temperature only
Ipsilateral loss of all sensory modalities only
e: Corticospinal and dorsal column fibres cross in the medulla, so their loss is ipsilateral. Spinothalamic fibres cross within one or two segments of entry, so pain and temperature loss is contralateral.
p: Anterior cord syndrome: loss of motor function and pain/temperature with preserved proprioception. Central cord syndrome: arms weaker than legs, often after a hyperextension injury.

q: Which antibody is most specific for rheumatoid arthritis?
e: Anti-CCP has specificity above 95% for RA and predicts erosive disease. Rheumatoid factor is less specific; it occurs in other conditions and in healthy older people.
p: Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are specific for SLE. Anti-histone antibodies suggest drug-induced lupus.

q: The best initial screening test for phaeochromocytoma is:
e: Plasma free metanephrines (or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines) have the highest sensitivity. Imaging (CT/MRI) is done only after biochemical confirmation.
p: Before surgery, give alpha-blockade first (phenoxybenzamine) and add a beta-blocker only after it; unopposed alpha stimulation can cause a hypertensive crisis. Rule of 10s (traditional): ~10% bilateral, extra-adrenal or malignant.

q: A serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) of 1.1 g/dL or more indicates:
e: A high SAAG reflects increased hydrostatic pressure in the portal circulation: cirrhosis, alcoholic hepatitis, cardiac ascites, Budd-Chiari syndrome. Low SAAG (<1.1) suggests peritoneal disease such as TB, malignancy or pancreatitis.
p: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis = ascitic fluid neutrophil count ≥250 cells/mm³. Cefotaxime is commonly used; albumin reduces the risk of renal failure.

q: A 60 kg adult has 30% total body surface area burns. By the Parkland formula, how much crystalloid is needed in the first 8 hours from the time of the burn?
e: Parkland: 4 mL × weight (kg) × %TBSA = 4 × 60 × 30 = 7200 mL in 24 hours. Half (3600 mL) is given in the first 8 hours from the time of injury and the rest over the next 16 hours. Ringer's lactate is used.
p: Titrate fluid to urine output (about 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults, 1 mL/kg/h in children). Rule of nines: each upper limb 9%, each lower limb 18%, anterior trunk 18%, posterior trunk 18%, head 9%, perineum 1%.

q: Charcot's triad of ascending cholangitis consists of fever with rigors, jaundice and:
e: Charcot's triad is fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. Adding hypotension and altered mental status gives Reynolds' pentad, which indicates severe (suppurative) cholangitis.
p: Management: resuscitation, antibiotics, and biliary drainage by ERCP. Courvoisier's law: a palpable gallbladder with jaundice is unlikely to be due to stones.

q: The most common malignancy of the thyroid gland is:
e: Papillary carcinoma accounts for most thyroid cancers. It spreads by lymphatics and has an excellent prognosis. Nuclear features include Orphan Annie eye nuclei, grooves and pseudo-inclusions.
p: Follicular carcinoma spreads by blood (bone, lung) and needs capsular or vascular invasion for diagnosis, so FNAC cannot tell it from adenoma. Medullary carcinoma arises from C cells, secretes calcitonin, and occurs in MEN 2.

q: A hernia that protrudes through Hesselbach's triangle is a:
e: Hesselbach's triangle is bounded by the inferior epigastric vessels laterally, the lateral border of rectus abdominis medially and the inguinal ligament inferiorly. A direct hernia passes through it, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
p: An indirect hernia passes through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. A femoral hernia lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle and is the most likely to strangulate.

q: In a haemodynamically STABLE patient with blunt abdominal trauma, the investigation of choice is:
e: CECT defines solid-organ injury grade and retroperitoneal injury in stable patients, guiding non-operative management. FAST is the bedside tool in UNSTABLE patients; a positive FAST with instability warrants laparotomy.
p: The spleen is the most commonly injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma; the liver is the most common in penetrating trauma.

q: According to Goodsall's rule, a fistula-in-ano with an external opening behind a transverse line through the anus usually:
o: Follows a curved track to an internal opening in the posterior midline
Runs straight radially to the nearest crypt
e: Posterior external openings usually follow a curved track to the posterior midline. Anterior openings, within about 3 cm of the anus, usually run radially in a straight line to the nearest crypt.
p: MRI pelvis is the investigation of choice for complex fistulas. A seton is used for high fistulas to preserve sphincter function.

q: On the Glasgow Coma Scale, a patient whose best motor response is withdrawal from a painful stimulus scores:
e: Motor scale: 6 obeys commands, 5 localises pain, 4 withdraws (normal flexion), 3 abnormal flexion (decorticate), 2 extension (decerebrate), 1 none.
p: GCS 8 or less = consider securing the airway (intubation). Eye opening is scored out of 4 and verbal response out of 5, so total GCS ranges from 3 to 15.

q: A 15-year-old boy presents with sudden severe scrotal pain for 3 hours. The testis is high-riding with a horizontal lie, and the cremasteric reflex is absent. The next step is:
o: Wait for a Doppler scan the next morning
e: This is testicular torsion until proven otherwise. Salvage rates are highest within about 6 hours, so clinical suspicion warrants immediate exploration. Detorsion and bilateral orchidopexy are done if viable; a non-viable testis is removed.
p: Prehn sign (pain relief on elevation) suggests epididymitis but is unreliable. The 'blue dot sign' is torsion of the appendix testis.

q: The drug of choice to control and prevent convulsions in eclampsia is:
e: Magnesium sulphate is superior to diazepam and phenytoin in preventing recurrent eclamptic fits. Pritchard and Zuspan regimens are commonly used.
p: Monitor for MgSO4 toxicity: loss of patellar reflex (first sign), respiratory rate <12/min, urine output <30 mL/h. Antidote: 10% calcium gluconate IV.

q: The most common cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage is:
e: Atony accounts for most cases of PPH. The '4 Ts' are Tone (atony), Trauma, Tissue (retained products) and Thrombin (coagulopathy).
p: Active management of the third stage of labour (uterotonic, controlled cord traction, uterine massage) prevents PPH. Oxytocin 10 IU IM is the uterotonic of choice. Tranexamic acid within 3 hours reduces deaths from bleeding.

q: Which of the following is NOT a component of the Bishop score?
e: The Bishop score assesses cervical dilatation, effacement (or length), consistency, position and station of the presenting part. A score of 8 or more suggests a favourable cervix for induction.
p: An unfavourable cervix is ripened before induction with prostaglandins (dinoprostone, misoprostol) or a Foley catheter.

q: The hormone detected by a standard urine pregnancy test is:
e: Pregnancy tests detect the beta subunit of hCG, made by the syncytiotrophoblast. It peaks at about 8-10 weeks. In a viable early intrauterine pregnancy, serum beta-hCG roughly doubles every 48 hours.
p: Very high hCG suggests molar pregnancy or multiple gestation. The discriminatory zone for a TVS-visible intrauterine sac is about 1500-2000 mIU/mL (thresholds vary).

q: Under the Rotterdam criteria, polycystic ovary syndrome is diagnosed when how many of the three features are present (after excluding other causes)?
o: Only ovarian morphology plus raised LH
e: The three Rotterdam features are oligo- or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound. Two of three are required, after excluding thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, non-classic CAH and others.
p: Letrozole is now generally first-line for ovulation induction in PCOS. Metformin helps insulin resistance. Unopposed oestrogen from anovulation raises the risk of endometrial hyperplasia.

q: The Copper-T 380A intrauterine device is approved for use for:
e: CuT 380A is licensed for 10 years (studies show effectiveness for even longer). Cu 375 is approved for 5 years. The LNG-IUS is approved for 5 years or more depending on the product.
p: An IUCD can be inserted within 5 days of unprotected intercourse as emergency contraception, the most effective method for that purpose.

q: The most common site of ectopic pregnancy is the:
e: Most ectopic pregnancies are tubal, and the ampulla is the most common site. Interstitial (cornual) ectopics rupture later but bleed catastrophically.
p: Methotrexate is suitable for a stable patient with an unruptured ectopic, low beta-hCG and no fetal cardiac activity. A haemodynamically unstable patient needs surgery.

q: The HPV types most strongly associated with cervical carcinoma are:
e: High-risk HPV 16 and 18 cause about 70% of cervical cancers. Their E6 and E7 proteins inactivate p53 and Rb respectively. Types 6 and 11 cause genital warts.
p: The transformation zone is where most cervical cancers arise. WHO recommends HPV DNA testing as the preferred primary screening test. HPV vaccination is best given before sexual debut.

q: A child can copy a circle at about:
e: Typical drawing milestones: vertical line at about 2 years, circle at 3 years, cross at 4 years, square at 4-5 years, triangle at 5 years.
p: Also at 3 years: rides a tricycle, knows full name and gender, and goes up stairs with alternating feet.

q: Social smile is expected to appear by:
e: A responsive social smile emerges at about 6-8 weeks. Its absence by 3 months warrants assessment of vision, hearing and development.
p: Laughs aloud at about 4 months. Stranger anxiety at about 7-9 months. Waves bye-bye at about 9-10 months.

q: Neonatal jaundice is most likely to be pathological when it:
o: Appears within the first 24 hours of life
Appears on day 3 in a term baby
Is unconjugated and below phototherapy thresholds
e: Jaundice within 24 hours suggests haemolysis (Rh or ABO incompatibility, G6PD deficiency) or infection, and needs urgent evaluation. Physiological jaundice appears after 24 hours, peaks on days 3-5 in term babies and resolves by about 2 weeks.
p: Other red flags: conjugated bilirubin above 1 mg/dL (or more than 20% of total), pale stools, rapidly rising bilirubin, or jaundice persisting beyond 2 weeks in a term baby (3 weeks in preterm).

q: Which is NOT one of the four classic components of tetralogy of Fallot?
e: The four features are VSD, RVOT obstruction (pulmonary stenosis), overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy. The addition of an ASD is called pentalogy of Fallot.
p: Chest X-ray shows a 'boot-shaped' heart. Hypercyanotic (tet) spells: knee-chest position, oxygen, morphine, IV fluids, phenylephrine, propranolol.

q: Small white spots on a red base on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars, appearing before the rash, are pathognomonic of:
e: Koplik spots appear 1-2 days before the measles rash and fade as it appears. The rash starts behind the ears and along the hairline and spreads downwards.
p: Vitamin A reduces measles mortality and complications. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a late complication. Rubella: postauricular lymphadenopathy, Forchheimer spots.

q: A healthy term infant's birth weight approximately TRIPLES by:
e: Birth weight roughly doubles by 4-5 months, triples by 1 year and quadruples by 2 years.
p: Length increases by about 50% by 1 year. Head circumference rises from about 35 cm at birth to about 45 cm at 1 year.

q: A 2-year-old has a barking cough, inspiratory stridor and hoarseness, and a neck X-ray shows a 'steeple sign'. The most common causative agent is:
e: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is mostly caused by parainfluenza virus type 1. Subglottic narrowing produces the steeple sign on AP neck X-ray.
p: Treat with a single dose of oral dexamethasone; nebulised adrenaline for moderate to severe stridor. Thumb sign on lateral X-ray = epiglottitis (Hib).

q: The feature that distinguishes kwashiorkor from marasmus is the presence of:
e: Kwashiorkor is characterised by oedema, flaky-paint dermatosis, hair changes, a fatty liver and apathy. Marasmus shows severe wasting with no oedema and the child is often alert and hungry.
p: Bilateral pitting oedema of nutritional origin classifies a child as having severe acute malnutrition regardless of weight. Other SAM criteria: weight-for-height below -3 SD, or MUAC below 11.5 cm.

q: The nerve most commonly injured in a supracondylar fracture of the humerus in children is the:
e: The anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve is most commonly affected in extension-type fractures. Patients cannot make an 'OK' sign because flexor pollicis longus and the index FDP are weak. Ulnar nerve injury is most common after medial pin placement.
p: Volkmann's ischaemic contracture can complicate supracondylar fractures. Pain on passive finger extension is the earliest sign of compartment syndrome.

q: The Garden classification is used for:
e: Garden grades femoral neck fractures I-IV by displacement. Grades III and IV (displaced) have a high risk of avascular necrosis and non-union, and are often treated with arthroplasty in older patients.
p: Pauwels classification uses the angle of the femoral neck fracture line. Schatzker classification is for tibial plateau fractures.

q: Sunburst appearance and Codman's triangle on X-ray around the knee in a teenager suggest:
e: Osteosarcoma arises in the metaphysis around the knee in adolescents. It produces aggressive periosteal reaction: radiating spicules (sunburst) and Codman's triangle.
p: Ewing sarcoma: diaphysis, 'onion-peel' periosteal reaction, t(11;22). Lungs are the most common site of metastasis for osteosarcoma.

q: An eccentric, lytic, 'soap-bubble' lesion at the end of a long bone in a 30-year-old, after closure of the growth plate, is most likely a:
e: Giant cell tumour is epiphyseal, extending to the subchondral bone in skeletally mature patients, most commonly around the knee (distal femur, proximal tibia) and distal radius.
p: Chondroblastoma is epiphyseal but occurs BEFORE growth plate closure. Osteoid osteoma causes night pain relieved by aspirin or NSAIDs, with a nidus under 2 cm.

q: Tuberculosis of the spine (Pott's disease) most commonly affects the:
o: Lower thoracic and upper lumbar (thoracolumbar) region
e: Spinal TB most commonly involves the lower thoracic and upper lumbar vertebrae. The paradiscal type (adjacent vertebral bodies and the disc between them) is the commonest.
p: Spinal TB is the most common site of skeletal TB. Pott's paraplegia may need surgical decompression. Cold abscess can track to form a psoas abscess.

q: The preferred initial treatment for idiopathic congenital talipes equinovarus (clubfoot) in a newborn is:
e: The Ponseti method uses gentle manipulation and serial long-leg casts, usually followed by percutaneous tenotomy of the Achilles tendon and then foot abduction braces. It corrects most clubfeet.
p: Order of correction in Ponseti (CAVE): Cavus, Adductus, Varus, Equinus. Equinus is corrected last. Brace compliance prevents relapse.

q: Foot drop after a fracture of the neck of the fibula is due to injury of the:
e: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve winds superficially around the fibular neck. Injury paralyses the ankle and toe dorsiflexors and the evertors, causing foot drop and a high-stepping gait, with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot.
p: The common peroneal is the most commonly injured nerve in the lower limb. A tight plaster cast at the fibular neck is also a cause.

q: A fracture of the proximal third of the ulna with dislocation of the radial head is called:
e: Monteggia: proximal ulna fracture with radial head dislocation. Galeazzi: distal radius shaft fracture with distal radioulnar joint dislocation.
p: Mnemonic MUGR: Monteggia = Ulna fracture; Galeazzi = Radius fracture. Posterior interosseous nerve injury can complicate a Monteggia fracture.

q: Pinpoint bleeding on scraping off the scales of a well-defined erythematous plaque is called:
e: Removing psoriatic scales exposes dilated capillaries in elongated dermal papillae beneath a thin suprapapillary epidermis, producing pinpoint bleeding.
p: Other psoriasis signs: candle-grease sign, Koebner phenomenon (lesions at sites of trauma), nail pitting, oil-drop sign. Munro microabscesses lie in the stratum corneum.

q: Flaccid blisters, painful oral erosions and a positive Nikolsky sign in a middle-aged adult suggest pemphigus vulgaris. The target antigen is:
e: Pemphigus vulgaris is caused by IgG against desmoglein 3 (plus desmoglein 1 in mucocutaneous disease). Loss of keratinocyte adhesion (acantholysis) produces suprabasal intraepidermal blisters. Direct IF shows a 'fishnet' intercellular pattern.
p: Bullous pemphigoid: elderly, tense subepidermal blisters, BP180/BP230, linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane. Pemphigus foliaceus: desmoglein 1, superficial blisters, no oral lesions.

q: Fine white lines (Wickham's striae) on the surface of violaceous, flat-topped, polygonal, itchy papules are seen in:
e: Lichen planus lesions are described by the 6 Ps: purple, polygonal, planar, pruritic papules and plaques. Wickham's striae reflect focal thickening of the granular layer.
p: Histology shows a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction, and Civatte (colloid) bodies. Associated with hepatitis C. Oral lesions have a lacy, reticular pattern.

q: The topical treatment of choice for scabies is:
e: Permethrin 5% is applied from the neck down (including the scalp in infants and the elderly), left overnight and repeated after 1 week. All close contacts are treated at the same time.
p: Oral ivermectin is used for crusted (Norwegian) scabies and institutional outbreaks. Burrows are typical in finger webs, wrists and genitalia, with itch that is worse at night.

q: Under WHO multidrug therapy, the standard duration of treatment for multibacillary leprosy in adults is:
e: WHO recommends rifampicin, clofazimine and dapsone for 12 months for MB leprosy. The same three drugs are recommended for 6 months for PB leprosy.
p: Type 1 (reversal) reaction affects nerves and skin; treat with steroids. Type 2 reaction (ENL) is immune complex mediated. Single-dose rifampicin is used as post-exposure prophylaxis for contacts.

q: Intensely itchy grouped vesicles on the elbows, knees and buttocks with granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae are associated with:
e: Dermatitis herpetiformis is the skin manifestation of coeliac disease. Antibodies target epidermal transglutaminase (TG3).
p: Dapsone controls the itch quickly. A gluten-free diet treats both skin and gut disease and lowers lymphoma risk.

q: A boggy, painful, pustular swelling of the scalp with hair loss in a child is most likely:
e: Kerion is a severe inflammatory host response to dermatophytes, often zoophilic species. It needs systemic antifungals (griseofulvin or terbinafine); topical agents alone do not reach the hair follicle.
p: Untreated kerion can cause scarring alopecia. Wood's lamp shows green fluorescence with Microsporum infection but not with most Trichophyton infections.

q: In herpes zoster ophthalmicus, vesicles on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson's sign) indicate involvement of the:
o: Nasociliary nerve, with high risk of ocular involvement
e: The nasociliary branch of the ophthalmic division supplies both the tip of the nose and the globe. Its involvement predicts eye complications such as keratitis and uveitis.
p: Start oral antivirals (acyclovir, valacyclovir) within 72 hours of rash onset, and refer to an ophthalmologist. Ramsay Hunt syndrome = zoster of the geniculate ganglion with facial palsy and vesicles in the ear.

q: 'First-rank symptoms' of schizophrenia were described by:
e: Schneider's first-rank symptoms include audible thoughts, third-person voices discussing or commenting on the patient, thought insertion, withdrawal and broadcasting, delusional perception, and made (passivity) experiences.
p: Bleuler coined the term 'schizophrenia' and the 4 As. Kraepelin called it 'dementia praecox'.

q: Polyuria and polydipsia in a patient on long-term lithium are most often due to:
e: Lithium accumulates in collecting duct cells and reduces their response to ADH (downregulating aquaporin-2), causing nephrogenic DI. Amiloride can reduce lithium entry into these cells.
p: Other lithium effects: hypothyroidism, tremor, weight gain, Ebstein anomaly if used in the first trimester. Toxicity is increased by thiazides, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and dehydration.

q: Delirium tremens typically begins how long after the last drink?
e: Simple withdrawal (tremor, sweating, anxiety) starts within 6-24 hours. Withdrawal seizures peak at 12-48 hours. Delirium tremens, with confusion, hallucinations and autonomic hyperactivity, usually begins at 48-72 hours.
p: Benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide, or lorazepam in liver disease) are the treatment. Give thiamine before glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.

q: The adverse effect of clozapine that requires regular blood count monitoring is:
e: Clozapine can cause potentially fatal neutropenia and agranulocytosis, so absolute neutrophil counts are monitored (weekly at first). Clozapine is the drug of choice for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
p: Other clozapine effects: hypersalivation, seizures (dose-related), myocarditis, constipation and ileus, weight gain. It rarely causes extrapyramidal symptoms.

q: The first-line drug for ADHD in school-age children is:
e: Stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamines) are first-line for ADHD. Atomoxetine (a non-stimulant) is an alternative, especially where there is a risk of substance misuse.
p: Stimulant effects to monitor: appetite suppression, insomnia, growth slowing, raised heart rate and BP.

q: The treatment of choice for severe depression with active suicidal risk or catatonia is:
e: ECT acts quickly and is highly effective in severe depression with suicidality, psychotic features, food refusal or catatonia. Benzodiazepines (lorazepam) are first-line for catatonia, with ECT if they fail.
p: ECT has no absolute contraindications. Raised intracranial pressure is the most important relative contraindication. Common side effects are transient memory impairment and headache.

q: The classic triad of Wernicke encephalopathy is:
e: Wernicke encephalopathy results from thiamine deficiency. The complete triad is present in a minority of patients, so treat on clinical suspicion with parenteral thiamine.
p: Korsakoff syndrome follows if untreated: anterograde amnesia with confabulation. The mammillary bodies are characteristically affected.

q: A patient on haloperidol develops high fever, generalised 'lead-pipe' rigidity, fluctuating BP and a markedly raised creatine kinase. The diagnosis is:
e: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is caused by dopamine D2 blockade. It develops over days with rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability and altered consciousness. Stop the antipsychotic, cool and hydrate the patient; dantrolene and bromocriptine may be used.
p: Serotonin syndrome develops within hours of a serotonergic drug, with clonus and hyperreflexia, and is treated with cyproheptadine.

q: Which inhalational anaesthetic has the lowest blood:gas partition coefficient (fastest induction and recovery)?
e: Desflurane has a blood:gas coefficient of about 0.42, lower than nitrous oxide (about 0.47), sevoflurane (about 0.65), isoflurane (about 1.4) and halothane (about 2.4). A lower coefficient means faster induction and recovery.
p: Sevoflurane is the agent of choice for inhalational induction because it is sweet and non-irritant. Desflurane irritates the airways and needs a heated vaporiser.

q: The specific drug for treatment of malignant hyperthermia is:
e: Dantrolene blocks ryanodine receptor (RyR1) calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Also stop the triggering agent, hyperventilate with 100% oxygen, and cool the patient.
p: Triggers: volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine. The earliest sign is often an unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2. It is linked to RYR1 mutations (autosomal dominant).

q: Succinylcholine should be avoided in a patient with:
o: An elective appendicectomy in a healthy adult
Rapid sequence intubation with a full stomach
e: After burns, crush injury, denervation or prolonged immobilisation, extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors proliferate. Succinylcholine can then cause life-threatening hyperkalaemia. The risk is highest from about 48 hours to many months after injury.
p: Succinylcholine is a depolarising relaxant with the fastest onset and shortest duration. Prolonged block occurs with pseudocholinesterase deficiency (dibucaine number).

q: Which local anaesthetic is the most cardiotoxic?
e: Bupivacaine binds cardiac sodium channels avidly and dissociates slowly, so it can cause refractory arrhythmias and cardiovascular collapse. Ropivacaine and levobupivacaine are less cardiotoxic.
p: Treat LA systemic toxicity with 20% lipid emulsion. Maximum doses: plain lignocaine 3 mg/kg, lignocaine with adrenaline 7 mg/kg, bupivacaine 2 mg/kg.

q: The Mallampati classification assesses:
o: Visibility of oropharyngeal structures with the mouth open, to predict difficult intubation
e: With the patient sitting, mouth fully open and tongue protruded, class I shows soft palate, fauces, uvula and pillars, while class IV shows the hard palate only. Higher classes predict difficult laryngoscopy.
p: Cormack-Lehane grades the glottic view at laryngoscopy. A thyromental distance under 6 cm suggests difficult intubation.

q: In a hypotensive trauma patient, the induction agent that best maintains blood pressure is:
e: Ketamine stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, maintaining heart rate and blood pressure. It is also a bronchodilator. Propofol and thiopentone cause vasodilation and myocardial depression.
p: Ketamine produces dissociative anaesthesia with analgesia. Emergence reactions are reduced by benzodiazepines. It increases salivation and has traditionally been avoided with raised intracranial pressure.

q: The most reliable method of confirming correct endotracheal tube placement is:
e: A persistent CO2 waveform over several breaths confirms tracheal placement. Clinical signs such as chest rise and breath sounds can be misleading. During cardiac arrest, CO2 may be low but a waveform is still seen with good CPR.
p: Sudden loss of ETCO2: circuit disconnection, oesophageal intubation, tube dislodgement or cardiac arrest. A rising ETCO2 during CPR suggests return of spontaneous circulation.

q: In adult CPR, chest compressions should be delivered at a rate of:
e: Current guidelines recommend 100-120 compressions per minute at a depth of 5-6 cm, allowing full recoil and minimising interruptions. The compression-to-ventilation ratio without an advanced airway is 30:2.
p: Shockable rhythms: VF and pulseless VT. Adrenaline 1 mg every 3-5 minutes. Amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock.

q: The most radiosensitive phase of the cell cycle is:
e: Cells are most radiosensitive in late G2 and mitosis, and most radioresistant in late S phase.
p: Law of Bergonié and Tribondeau: tissues with high mitotic rate and less differentiation are more radiosensitive. The 4 Rs of radiobiology are Repair, Reoxygenation, Redistribution and Repopulation.

q: The initial investigation of choice for suspected acute subarachnoid haemorrhage is:
e: NCCT is highly sensitive in the first hours after SAH, showing hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns and sulci. If CT is negative and suspicion is high, lumbar puncture looks for xanthochromia. Angiography (CTA or DSA) then locates the aneurysm.
p: Nimodipine is given to reduce delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm. A 'thunderclap headache' (worst headache of life) is the classic presentation.

q: The SI unit of equivalent (and effective) dose is the:
e: Sievert accounts for the biological effect of the radiation type (and, for effective dose, the tissue). The Gray is the unit of absorbed dose (1 J/kg). The Becquerel measures radioactivity (1 disintegration per second).
p: ICRP occupational dose limit: 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years. Public limit: 1 mSv per year.

q: A perihilar 'bat-wing' pattern of opacity on chest X-ray is classically seen in:
e: Alveolar pulmonary oedema fills the central (perihilar) airspaces bilaterally, sparing the periphery and producing a bat-wing or butterfly pattern.
p: Other CXR signs of cardiac failure: upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, cardiomegaly, pleural effusions and peribronchial cuffing.

q: The best plain radiograph for detecting a small amount of free intraperitoneal air is:
e: On an erect chest film, gas collects under the domes of the diaphragm and as little as 1-2 mL can be seen. Keeping the patient upright for about 10 minutes before the film improves sensitivity. CT is the most sensitive test overall.
p: If the patient cannot stand, use a left lateral decubitus film. Rigler's sign (both sides of the bowel wall visible) is seen on supine films with a large pneumoperitoneum.

q: The most sensitive imaging test for early acute osteomyelitis is:
e: MRI detects marrow oedema within days of infection. Plain X-ray changes (periosteal reaction, lysis) usually take 10-14 days to appear.
p: Sequestrum = dead bone. Involucrum = new periosteal bone around it. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause; Salmonella is classically associated with sickle cell disease.

q: The physical half-life of technetium-99m is about:
e: Tc-99m emits 140 keV gamma rays with a 6-hour half-life, which is ideal for imaging. It is obtained from a molybdenum-99 generator.
p: I-131 has a half-life of about 8 days. F-18 (FDG-PET) has a half-life of about 110 minutes.

q: A 'coffee bean' sign on an abdominal radiograph of an elderly man with abdominal distension suggests:
e: A massively dilated, twisted sigmoid loop forms an inverted-U 'coffee bean' shape arising from the pelvis. Contrast enema shows a 'bird's beak' at the point of twist.
p: For sigmoid volvulus without peritonitis, the first-line treatment is endoscopic (flexible sigmoidoscopic) decompression, followed by elective resection because of recurrence.
